children: Micron Technology
has reportedly suspended construction of a
$4.5 billion memory-chip plant in Taiwan
as a prolonged labor dispute threatens one of the company's most important manufacturing hubs.
The project, known as
Fab 11E
, was being built in Taoyuan and had been expected to come online in 2028. Bloomberg reported that Micron had budgeted roughly
$3 billion to $4.5 billion
for the complex, including advanced equipment purchases, but construction is now largely being frozen apart from limited safety work.
The dispute centers on employee compensation.
Micron's Taoyuan union is pushing for a permanent profit-sharing framework and has demanded that
15% of operating profit be distributed to employees globally
, while also favoring cash incentives over stock-based compensation. The union secured strike authorization last month, with
99% of nearly 2,000 voting members supporting the move

Micron did reach an agreement with its larger Taichung union in October, but some workers are now challenging those terms and the Taoyuan union is trying to expand its representation and reopen negotiations.
The stakes are unusually high because Taiwan is central to Micron's supply chain.
The island accounts for roughly
60% of Micron's global DRAM output
and also produces a large share of its high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, used in AI accelerators and servers. Micron employs about
15,000 people in Taiwan
, making it the company's largest workforce base.
For now, there is no indication that existing production has been disrupted. Micron has said its current Taiwan operations remain normal and that it is confident in maintaining customer continuity.
Investor Takeaway
I think the key distinction is that
this is a future-capacity problem, not yet a current-production problem
Micron's existing HBM and DRAM output has not been shut down. But if Fab 11E is delayed materially, one of the company's planned supply additions could slip at exactly the wrong time.
That could actually cut both ways.
For Micron, delayed capacity may limit future volume growth. But in a market already struggling with memory shortages, slower supply additions could also keep pricing stronger for longer.
That is why the labor dispute matters more than the $4.5 billion headline alone.
For investors, the key things to watch are
whether construction resumes, whether either union escalates toward an actual strike, how Micron reallocates capex, and whether the delay changes its HBM and DRAM supply outlook through 2028
The immediate risk is operational uncertainty.
The bigger question is whether it tightens an already constrained memory market even further.

title: Micron's Bold Memory Expansion Faces a Sudden Crisis
